verified_ref: Dohavali 84 (Gita Press, Poddar); also 84 in Kali Prasad Shastri's Kaumudi tika
translation_note: Our rendering drops the conditional: both commentaries read 'tau' as 'if this is so, then'. Consider 'if I am yours alone, then Tulsi is well...'. Minor.
context: Gita Press prints this doha under the heading 'the glory of taking refuge' (sharanagati), right after two dohas warning that sense-pleasures make devotion taste flat. It opens a run of short self-portraits in which Tulsidas sets his faults against his reliance on Ram; doha 85 follows directly.

key_terms.sense: such as I am, good or bad, whatever my condition
in all three worlds and all three times (past, present, future)

core_teaching: If Tulsi truly belongs to Ram alone, whatever his quality, then his welfare is secure everywhere and always. Belonging, not merit, is the ground of safety.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as a conditional: if it is true that this Tulsidas, good or bad, is Ram's alone, then he fares well wherever he is and in every time; footnotes Gita 4.11 (the Lord meets people as they approach him).

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Same conditional sense: whatever I am, if I remain only yours, all is well in every world and time; otherwise there is nothing but trouble.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate worth from belonging: you do not have to become good first to be held; the work is to keep turning toward the one you trust.
misreadings: Not a claim that Tulsi is already virtuous; it explicitly sets aside the question of quality.
Not a guarantee of outward success; the 'well-being' is the commentaries' kalyan (ultimate good).
cautions: Mild: 'only yours' language can feel exclusive to readers of other faiths; keep the focus on belonging rather than on rejecting other refuges.
not_for: someone who needs practical help today rather than reassurance
readers hostile to exclusive devotional language

verified_ref: Dohavali 85 (Gita Press); 85 in Kali Prasad Shastri
context: Follows doha 84 in the same 'refuge' cluster. Tulsidas concedes the public verdict on him and names the one quality he can claim; the next doha (86) defines devotion as love for Ram plus walking the path of right conduct.
core_teaching: Even a person widely seen as full of faults has one thing that can please God: wholehearted trust.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Paraphrase: people call me a storehouse of faults, but I have one quality, complete trust in you; therefore it is fitting that you be pleased with me.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Adds that the world finds nothing in Tulsi to admire, and he agrees; yet his one great quality is trust in Sita-Ram, who know only how to do good. However bad I am, I know what pleases you.

practical_reading: Used to encourage people who feel defined by others' judgement: you may not be able to argue with every criticism, but you can still bring trust.
misreadings: Not permission to ignore real faults; the neighbouring dohas (86-88) immediately call for right conduct and honest speech.
Not self-pity; the tone is wry and confident.
cautions: Could reinforce harsh self-talk if the reader is already self-critical; emphasise the 'one virtue' half.
speaks_to: feeling you have nothing to offer
not_for: someone being unfairly scapegoated who needs validation that the accusations are wrong
readers in a shame spiral, if read without the second line

verified_ref: Dohavali 95 (Gita Press). Kali Prasad Shastri also numbers it 95 but reads a variant first word.
translation_note: 'Without conditions' for nirupadhi is acceptable but Gita Press says 'without guile/deceit' (sincerely, without pretence). 'Hold Ram in awe' is a fair softening of 'fear'.
context: Gita Press heads this doha 'exhortation' (udbodhan). It comes just after Tulsi's self-accusing dohas and before 96, the advice to tell Ram everything. It is a compact rule of devotional life addressed to oneself.

key_terms.sense: fear (hold in awe) Ram alone; variant 'ramahi ura karu' = keep Ram in your heart
without pretext, pretence or ulterior motive; Gita Press glosses 'without guile'

core_teaching: Direct awe, love, attachment and trust to Ram, and be his without pretence; then even outward loss counts as winning.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Fear only Ram, place mamata, love and trust in him; for one who is Ram's servant without deceit, even losing is winning.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Prints 'ramahi ura karu' (hold Ram in the heart) instead of 'daru' (fear); explains that worshipping the attribute-free Ram brings victory even when one has not done bhajan well.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as consolation for setbacks: if your loyalty is undivided and sincere, a lost contest or failed plan is not the final word on you.
misreadings: Not 'losing doesn't matter, so don't try'; the doha is about the inner orientation that survives defeat.
'Fear Ram' is reverent awe, not terror of punishment.
cautions: Text variant: Gita Press 'daru' (fear) vs Kaumudi 'ura' (heart). If a writer builds on 'fear', note it is only one reading.
speaks_to: wanting to give oneself fully to something
not_for: someone being pressured to 'accept defeat' in an abusive or unjust situation
readers frightened of a punishing God
research_note: Textual variant 'ramahi daru' (GP) / 'ramahi ura' (Kaumudi tika) noted in OCR of both editions; worth an editor's eye.

verified_ref: Dohavali 96 (Gita Press); 96 in Kali Prasad Shastri
translation_note: 'Misery' for dinata is fine; Gita Press keeps 'dinata' (abjectness/wretchedness). Kaumudi tika variant 'saba dosha' (all faults) in place of 'guna dosha'.
context: Immediately follows 95 in the 'exhortation' group. Tulsi speaks to himself: having said that sincere belonging turns loss into victory, he now gives the practice, honest disclosure to a kind listener.

key_terms.sense: speak it out, tell it fully
merits and faults (Kaumudi reads 'saba dosha', all faults)
grow thin / grow plump: Tulsi's playful body imagery

core_teaching: Open your whole heart, merits and faults, to the compassionate Ram; abjectness will shrink and contentment will grow strong.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Tell gracious Ram all your merits and faults with an open heart; your dinata will become weak and your contentment will become very firm.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'tell all your faults'; says dinata will grow so lean that it cannot come near the stoutness of contentment.

practical_reading: Used as an image for confession, journaling or prayer: naming everything honestly to a kind presence lightens the weight more than hiding it.
misreadings: Not a promise that problems vanish by being spoken; what changes is the inner state (dinata vs santosha).
Not an instruction to disclose everything to any person; the listener is the 'kripalu' Ram.
speaks_to: starting a journaling or prayer practice
not_for: someone whose disclosures have been used against them, if read as 'tell people everything'

verified_ref: Dohavali 100 (Gita Press). Kali Prasad Shastri appears to number it 99 (OCR reads 'ninety-nine').
context: In Gita Press it closes a short run on reliance on Ram and is followed by dohas on the unity of Shiva and Ram. Kaumudi tika frames it as Tulsi's lament after devotees of other paths all criticised his way.

key_terms.sense: whatever good is to happen, will happen (from Ram)

core_teaching: In the world people mostly block each other; real good comes from the kind Ram.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: In this world everyone is a hindrance to everyone, nobody is anyone's helper; whatever good happens comes from kind Ram.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Situates it biographically: all the critics opposed my way and none supported it; now my trust is in Ram alone, let him do whatever good he will.

practical_reading: Read as permission to stop waiting for others' approval and to rest one's hope somewhere steadier.
misreadings: Not a blanket claim that all people are bad or that help from others should be refused.
Can sound cynical if lifted from its devotional frame.
cautions: For someone isolated or depressed, 'no one is a helper' may confirm a distorted belief; pair with encouragement to seek actual support.
speaks_to: opposition at work or in community
not_for: someone who is isolated and needs to be nudged toward people, not away from them
readers with paranoid or persecutory distress

verified_ref: Dohavali 147 in Gita Press (both scans) and 146 in Kali Prasad Shastri. NOT 101: Gita Press doha 101 is 'sankara priya mama drohi...' on Shiva-Ram unity.
attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Dohavali 147 (Gita Press), not 101.
context: Part of a Gita Press group on Ram's grace and protection (dohas 145-148). The image of the infant reaching for snake and fire is a favourite of Tulsi's; Gita Press notes the same picture in Ramcharitmanas Aranya Kand (the mother who pulls a child back from fire and snake).
core_teaching: As parents snatch an unknowing child away from a snake or fire, Sita and Ram guard the devotee who does not see the danger he is playing with.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: As parents stop a child playing with a snake or putting his hand in fire, so Sita-Ram, as mother and father, save the child Tulsi when he heads toward the snake or flame of sense-objects.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Mother and father of the world, Sita-Ram, protect the child playing with a serpent and reaching into fire, just as natural parents do.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to speak of unseen protection and of how much of our safety we never notice; the danger in the commentary is our own pull toward harmful pleasures.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will ever happen.
Not a reason to take risks because 'someone will catch me'.
cautions: A reader whose child was harmed, or who was not protected as a child, may find the parental image painful.
not_for: someone grieving a child's death or injury
survivors of childhood neglect or abuse, unless carefully framed
research_note: Gita Press scan 1 has its pages out of order in OCR; scan 2 prints the number 147 directly after the doha.

verified_ref: Dohavali 109 (Gita Press); about 108-109 in Kali Prasad Shastri
context: One of Tulsidas's autobiographical dohas, in a group on Ram's favour making the weak strong (doha 110 cites Hanuman's role in Sugriva's feud). It matches the begging-childhood verses of Kavitavali (Uttar 57, 73) and Hanuman Bahuk 29.

key_terms.sense: begged scraps/crusts from house to house

core_teaching: When Tulsi lived without Ram's shelter he begged for crusts; since Ram became his helper even kings honour him. The change of fortune is credited to grace, not to his own effort.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: When I was without Ram's support I begged scraps door to door; now that Ram is my helper, kings worship my feet.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Expands in verse: those who once begged crumbs without Ram are now helped by him and kings bow; for the one with Raghuvar in the heart, even gods bow.

practical_reading: Used as a story of reversal: where you start is not where you end, and the change can come from turning toward a source of strength.
misreadings: Not a prosperity promise (devotion = wealth and status).
The honour from kings is a sign of grace in the tradition, not the goal.
cautions: Poverty imagery: avoid implying that poor people lack God's help.
not_for: someone in present poverty who may hear it as 'you're poor because you lack faith'

verified_ref: Dohavali 175 in Gita Press (scan 2 prints the number) and 175 in Kali Prasad Shastri's index. NOT 143: Gita Press doha 143 is 'jani rama seva sarasa...' (Brahma became Jambavan, Shiva became Hanuman).
attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Dohavali 175 (Gita Press), not 143.
context: Follows doha 174, which lists Ram's grace turning a stone into Ahalya, floating rocks on the sea and reviving fallen monkeys; 176 asks Tulsi to remember the one whose messenger is Hanuman. Ahalya, cursed to stone, was freed by the touch of Ram's feet.

key_terms.sense: the feet that freed the stone (Ahalya) from her curse
the heart's hope will be fulfilled

core_teaching: Remember Ram's liberating feet, drop worry; trouble will pass and the heart's wish will be met.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Remember the feet of Ram that freed the stone-Ahalya from her curse and give up all anxiety; by such single-minded remembrance your troubles go and your wish is fulfilled.

practical_reading: Used as a short anti-anxiety practice: when worry loops, turn attention to a remembered act of mercy instead of the feared outcome.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that every wish comes true.
Not a dismissal of real problems that need action.
cautions: The Ahalya story involves deception and a husband's curse; avoid retelling details for readers with sexual-assault trauma.
Promise-of-fulfilment language should be softened.
not_for: someone whose prayers for a specific outcome (health, a child) were not answered
readers for whom the Ahalya story is triggering
research_note: Only one commentary (Gita Press) read cleanly; the Kaumudi tika index confirms 175 but its comment was not located in the OCR.

verified_ref: Dohavali 152 (Gita Press); 152 in Kali Prasad Shastri
translation_note: Our translation reverses the causation. Both commentaries read: with straight mind, speech and deeds, all the means that give birth to love for Raghubar become straight/easy. Ours says straightness is born OF love. Suggested: 'A straight mind, straight words, straight deeds: then every way to love for Raghubar is straight.' Fix the line too.
context: Gita Press heads it 'an easy means of gaining love for Ram'. The next doha (153) warns against a bright outward appearance and sweet speech hiding a bitter mind and dirty deeds.
core_teaching: For one whose mind, speech and deeds are straightforward, every means of gaining love for Ram becomes straight and easy. Guilelessness is the soil in which love grows.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: If mind, speech and all actions are simple, then every method that produces love for Raghunath is simple; love of God comes very easily through mind, word and deed free of hypocrisy.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: If the mind is guileless, speech clean and deeds praiseworthy, the whole method of producing love for Ram is straight; quotes Manas: the pure-hearted find me, I dislike deceit.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as integrity before piety: be the same inside and outside, and devotion stops being complicated.
misreadings: Not 'love makes you straight' (that reverses the causation in both commentaries).
Not a call to naivety; 'sudha' means without guile, not gullible.
not_for: someone in a manipulative environment who may hear it as 'just be simple and trusting'

verified_ref: Dohavali 256 (Gita Press); 256 in Kali Prasad Shastri's text (index lists 244, likely index error)
translation_note: Fine. 'True home' = paraloka/the divine home in Gita Press.
context: Gita Press heads it 'attachment, not householder life, is the obstacle to love of God'. Doha 255 just before warns false renunciants who throw away their begging gear; 257 praises staying at home with contentment.

key_terms.sense: by making a home (being a householder)
the city of love for Ram

core_teaching: Clinging to household life loses the true home; walking out of it loses the worldly home. Live in between, in the household but inwardly free, and build the city of Ram's love there.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Living as a householder loses one's real home (the next world); renouncing loses the home here; so live in the house like a renunciant and settle the city of Ram's love.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Two homes are meant, the natural and the divine; outwardly keep the household and its duties, renounce mentally, and at times retreat to solitude for bhajan; mere leaving home does not win God.

practical_reading: A balance teaching for people tempted either to over-identify with family and possessions or to escape them: stay, but hold it lightly.
misreadings: Not a rejection of family life; the heading says household life is not the obstacle.
Not an endorsement of walking out on responsibilities.
not_for: someone who needs to leave an unsafe home: this verse could be misread as 'don't leave'

verified_ref: Dohavali 278 (Gita Press); 278 in Kali Prasad Shastri
context: Second of Tulsi's famous chataka (rain-bird) series, which starts at 277. The chataka is said to drink only rain from one cloud (or the Svati raindrop) and so is the poets' figure of single-minded love. Doha 279 goes further: let the bird not even drink, since love's thirst is better growing.

key_terms.sense: the rain-bird that waits only for its cloud

core_teaching: Whether the beloved cloud rains on time or stays indifferent for a whole lifetime, the chataka-mind hopes only in it. Love does not depend on being answered.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: O cloud-Ram, whether you rain your grace on time or stay indifferent all my life and never rain, this mind-chataka has hope only in you.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Glosses in verse: the chataka mind never despairs, whether the cloud rains in season or never gives a drop.

practical_reading: Used for faith in dry seasons: continuing to hope and practise when prayer seems unanswered.
misreadings: Not advice to keep waiting on a person who ignores you (our misuse note already says so).
Not glorification of suffering for its own sake.
cautions: Could validate staying in a neglectful relationship if 'cloud' is read as a human partner.
speaks_to: long waiting (for a child, a job, healing)
not_for: someone in an emotionally neglectful relationship
someone told to keep waiting by an exploitative guru or partner

verified_ref: Dohavali 277 in Gita Press (scan 2 prints the number) and 277 in Kali Prasad Shastri. NOT 282.
attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Dohavali 277 (Gita Press and Kaumudi tika), not 282. Setting ('opening of the chataka dohas') is right.
context: Gita Press heads it 'Gosvamiji's single-mindedness' and prints it as the opening doha of the chataka series (277 onwards); 278 follows. The rain-bird that waits only for its one cloud stands for undivided devotion.
core_teaching: All of Tulsi's reliance, strength, hope and faith rest on one object, Ram the dark cloud, as the chataka depends on its one cloud.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: One trust, one strength, one hope and one faith: Tulsidas has become a chataka for the one dark cloud, Ram.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Versifies it: the chataka Tulsidas relies only on the one Ghanashyam; his strength, hope and faith are all in him.

practical_reading: A verse for focus and loyalty: stop scattering trust across many anxious sources and anchor it in one.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all human relationships.
'One' is devotional single-mindedness (ananyata), not exclusivism toward other people.
cautions: Exclusive devotional language; frame inclusively for a general audience.
not_for: someone being isolated by a controlling partner or group that demands 'only me'

verified_ref: Dohavali 405 (Gita Press); 405 in Kali Prasad Shastri
context: In Gita Press it sits in a run of worldly-wise dohas about the weak and the treacherous. Doha 404 says the weak find no place anywhere; 406 condemns those who swear friendship, learn the household's secrets and then plot, calling those who trust them doomed.

key_terms.sense: head in (his) lap: the image of sleeping in total trust
the protector is the Lord of the world

core_teaching: If the very person in whose lap you sleep in trust turns treacherous, only God can protect you from that.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: If the one in whose lap you trustingly lay your head to sleep plays a treacherous trick, then only God can protect you from it.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Adds a practical gloss: recognise an enemy and guard yourself alertly; if a friend plays foul, Ram protects and brings you through.

practical_reading: Read as consolation and as realism after betrayal by someone close: you could not have guarded against it, and you are not left alone.
misreadings: Not advice to stop protecting yourself (Kaumudi explicitly says stay alert).
Not blame on the betrayed for trusting.
cautions: Intimate betrayal may include abuse; do not let the verse replace practical safety steps (our misuse note is right).
Doha 406 nearby is harsh toward trusting people; do not pair them.
speaks_to: betrayal by a partner, friend or business associate
not_for: someone currently in danger from a partner who needs safety planning, not consolation alone

verified_ref: Dohavali 424 (Gita Press); about 424 in Kali Prasad Shastri (index 423)
translation_note: Fine. Our 'shield yourself' matches Gita Press's 'stand and block the blow'.
context: Gita Press heads it 'God protects everyone'. Doha 425 follows with 'fighting is to be wholly avoided': the wise avoid battle even with leaves and flowers, citing the Yadavas and Kama.

key_terms.sense: striking a wound (hitting back) is not good
Raghuraj (Ram) the guardian over every head

core_teaching: If attacked, escaping is fine and defending yourself is fine, but striking back is not; Ram stands guard over everyone's head.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: If someone attacks you it is good to run away, or to stand and block the blow for self-protection; but hitting back is not good, because Ram the protector is over everyone's head.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Running is good, taking cover is good, striking back is not; Ram guards all beings, and no one can kill the one he keeps.

practical_reading: Used as an ethic of non-retaliation that still allows self-protection: leave, shield yourself, but don't escalate.
misreadings: Not an instruction to endure abuse: the verse explicitly approves fleeing and self-defence.
Not pacifism that forbids protecting others.
cautions: For abuse victims, stress the first half (leaving and shielding are good).
'Over everyone's head' includes the attacker in the commentaries' reading; can feel unjust to a victim.
not_for: someone being told by family or clergy to 'not react' to ongoing abuse
victims of violence seeking justice

verified_ref: Dohavali 528 (Gita Press); 528 in Kali Prasad Shastri
translation_note: Translation fine. Our line adds 'out of love'; the doha's reason is 'knows his own dharma'. Consider 'Hanuman, who knew his own duty, simply leapt.'
context: Gita Press heads it 'an obedient servant is greater than the master'. Near the end of the Dohavali; the next doha (529) praises the banyan that grows in harmony with its root and gives to all without pride.

key_terms.sense: the servant is greater than the master

core_teaching: A servant who is expert in his own duty can surpass the master: Ram had to build a bridge to cross the ocean, Hanuman simply leapt it.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: The servant skilled in following his own dharma is greater than the master: Ram crossed the sea by building a bridge, Hanuman crossed the same sea by leaping.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: A servant who is skilled at his own work becomes especially strong: Hanuman leapt the sea while the king himself had to organise a great bridge-building.

practical_reading: Applied to service and teamwork: excellence in one's own role is a form of greatness, and the devotee's power is the Lord's gift showing through.
misreadings: Not a claim that Hanuman is greater than Ram in the theological sense.
'Out of love' (our line) is not in the doha; the stated reason is mastery of one's own dharma.
speaks_to: people in support roles who feel overlooked
pride in doing one's own work well
not_for: someone being exploited in a 'servant' role at work or home

verified_ref: Gitavali, Ayodhya Kand, pada 52 (Gita Press; same in Shrikant Sharan). Ref should carry the kand and number.
attribution_note: Ref field reads only 'Gitavali'; should be 'Gitavali, Ayodhya Kand 52'. Speaker is Tulsidas narrating Kausalya.
translation_note: Fine. Gita Press adds a verse about telling him to go to the king and eat, and the final frozen-picture line, which our excerpt omits.
context: After Ram has left for the forest, the Gitavali gives a series of songs on Kausalya's longing in the empty palace. In this pada she handles his childhood bow, arrows and little shoes, sometimes goes to wake him as before, sometimes calls him to eat, and then, remembering he has gone, stands frozen 'like a painted picture'. The next pada (53) has her saying she still cannot believe it is not a dream.

key_terms.sense: as before, as in the old days
stunned, like a figure in a painting

core_teaching: A mother's love keeps reaching for the absent child through his things and her old routines; the poem honours grief as love that has nowhere to go.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya looks at his play bow, presses his little shoes to heart and eyes, goes to wake him as before or calls him to eat, then stands stunned, remembering the exile; Tulsi says describing it shows his love is shallow.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Gitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Notes that in separation the beloved's belongings become as dear as the beloved, and touching them gives a taste of meeting; cross-references Bharat touching Ram's footprints in the Manas.

practical_reading: Teachers and readers use it to validate the rituals of grief, keeping things, keeping routines, as forms of love rather than failure to 'move on'.
misreadings: Not a lesson to detach or stop grieving; nothing in the poem corrects Kausalya.
Ram is alive in the story; the loss is absence, not death.
cautions: Very strong for empty-nest or separation grief; for a parent whose child has died it may be overwhelming. Ram returns in the story; a bereaved parent's child does not.
speaks_to: parents whose children have moved away
separation from a child (custody, migration, estrangement)
not_for: a parent in fresh bereavement for a child, unless chosen with great care
readers who need movement toward hope on the same day

verified_ref: Gitavali, Sundar Kand, pada 42 (Gita Press; Shrikant Sharan same)
translation_note: Fine. 'Royal road' = Gita Press 'path of devotion'.
context: Follows the Gitavali's telling of Vibhishan coming over to Ram and being welcomed (padas 40ff). Tulsi steps back to generalise: refuge in Ram is open to everyone. Later stanzas of the pada mention Ajamil saved by calling his son's name and Vibhishan's single bow bearing fruit.

key_terms.sense: those who went to Ram for refuge
Ram's royal highway (Gita Press: the path of devotion)

core_teaching: Taking refuge in Ram is good for everyone without exception: rich or poor, high or low, clever or dull, weak or strong, disabled or resourceless.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Everyone who goes to Ram's refuge is well off, rich or poor, great or small, wise or foolish, weak or mighty; even the lame, blind and resourceless who took Ram's highway of devotion were carried through.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Gitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Says this removes any eligibility test from surrender; cites Gita 9.32 that anyone, of any birth, reaches the highest by taking refuge; the royal road is protected as a king's road is policed.

practical_reading: Used as a statement of radical welcome: there is no entry requirement of status, intelligence, strength or ability.
misreadings: Not a claim that the disabled or poor are spiritually deficient; the point is that no condition excludes anyone.

survivors of parental abuse, without careful framing

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)

commentaries.who: Murari Madhusudan Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering
